summary: A stone light on Wisconsin's Long Tail Point in Green Bay, lit in 1848; LighthouseFriends says the first tower still stands, and the later lights are gone.

light.note: Lights in the first tower (1848), the 1859 house and the 1899 pier light; the last was destroyed in 1973.

structures.note: The first tower, the only one still standing (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record says it does not exist. Wikidata and Rowlett give 1849 for the build.
Sold in 1936 on condition it be moved; dismantled after the trailer broke through the ice.

structures.role: light on a concrete pier atop a wooden crib (third light)
structures.note: Destroyed by a storm on 9 April 1973.

access.note: Owned by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources; grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Best seen by boat or from the air.

facts.agency: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (owner, per LighthouseFriends); Long Tail Unit of the Green Bay West Shores Wildlife Area

events.note: Congress appropriates $5,000 for a light at the entrance to Green Bay; the Pottawatomie Island light is judged to serve it
Congress appropriates $4,000 for the Tail Point light; work begins with limestone from near Bay Settlement
Peter White activates the first stone tower (Wikidata and Rowlett give 1848 and 1849 for the build)
New octagonal lantern and sixth-order Fresnel lens (the USLHS record gives 1850 for the original lens)
Lake level rises and surrounds the stone tower; the Board builds a wooden house on higher ground and moves the lantern and lens into it
Fog bell placed in operation on 5 July
The Light-House Board says the fog bell is of little or no benefit where it is, and proposes moving the light and bell
Third light: a small frame house with lantern on a concrete pier atop a wooden crib; work begins 15 April; established 1 August 1899 (item 518); a changes-in-location entry gives 31 July 1899
Bell replaced by a five-inch compressed-air fog signal
Keeper C. Witzmann and first assistant A. Weber at Tail Point are credited with rescuing three men from a raft after a motorboat capsized and sank (the table entry is matched by position)
A storm floods Green Bay; keeper Witzmann is rescued by the tug Greiling after three hours (Lighthouse Friends only)
Light automated; the 1859 dwelling is sold for removal the same year
The surrounding land becomes the Long Tail Point Migratory Waterfowl Refuge; the 1859 dwelling is dismantled after breaking through the ice
Storm on 9 April destroys the 1899 tower and house
Light discontinued (USLHS); the first tower remains standing

wrecks.outcome: Capsized and sank; keeper Witzmann and assistant Weber rescued three men from a raft (fiscal year 1919)
Flood around Green Bay; the keeper was rescued by the tug Greiling after three hours

corrections.why: Green Island WI (ruins) is a separate light at Marinette, established 1863 and discontinued 1956. Its name should not be a name for this station.

These events come from uslhs:8996, which the roster tool identifies as the Green Island WI (ruins) record (nid 8996, Marinette), not this station. The station's own USLHS records are 8997, 9568 and 9569.

corrections.proposed: remove unless a source is found
corrections.why: The USLHS Tail Point New record and LighthouseFriends both give 1936 for automation; no source read supports 1933.
LighthouseFriends says the storm of 9 April 1973 destroyed the 1899 tower, which is more specific than the undated Wikidata end date.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS and LighthouseFriends give 1848 for the first light, and the Light-House Board's 1894 and 1899 references are to the later lights; the 1849 build date in Rowlett and OSM is treated as the completion of the tower.
The 1859 house was the second light and was replaced by the 1899 pier light, so the 1973 end date belongs to the 1899 light; the 1859 deactivation in Rowlett refers to the first tower's use.

notes_for_editor: Scan pages now verified for the Board items: 1894 item 1394 scan p. 487; 1899 item 501 scan p. 196; 1900 item 518 scan p. 171; 1900 changes in location scan p. 23 (31 July 1899). Disagreements now stated in the story: (1) red can buoy / new crib distance: the 1894 report gives 1,650 yards from the present light, LighthouseFriends gives 1,050 yards southeast; (2) move to the new structure: the 1900 report gives 1 August 1899 in item 518 and 31 July 1899 in its changes-in-location list; LighthouseFriends says 1 August; (3) tower date: USLHS record and most of LighthouseFriends say 1848 (activated 1848); LighthouseFriends' 1870s passage calls it the 1849 stone lighthouse; Rowlett and Wikidata (not read in the story) give 1849 for the build; (4) stone: LighthouseFriends says limestone; USLHS says sandstone; (5) status: USLHS ruins record says Existing: No; LighthouseFriends says the first tower still stands; (6) Witzmann: the USLHS roster has him principal keeper from 1910; LighthouseFriends dates his appointment to 1920; the fiscal 1919 Commissioner table already calls him keeper. The 1919 raft rescue: the Commissioner table prints its columns separately, so the Tail Point row and the raft entry are matched by POSITION (the table's vessel, nature-of-assistance and station blocks are not aligned in the OCR). The story says so. CHECK THE PAGE IMAGE (archive.org bub_gb_B2dYAAAAYAAJ, scan p. 463) before any change; the match to 'G. F. Laviolette' is LighthouseFriends' claim, not the table's. The 1929 flood rescue comes from LighthouseFriends only; no Bulletin or Commissioner corroboration was found. The 1859 house: LighthouseFriends says it was east of the stone tower; the story does not give a direction. The 1899 and 1900 Board items have no printed page confirmed; cited by scan page. USLHS roster counts (26 stints: 3 first tower, 7 second, 16 third) were counted and match the story. Gaylord: LighthouseFriends says forced to retire by a cancerous growth; the story gives no cause. Wikipedia not cited. One newspaper search (Chronicling America, Wisconsin, 1848-1900) found nothing useful about the light, per the earlier research run.
